content:
I really don't get why you closed my PRs, most of them were in draft, you didn't need to review them right away.

AI assisted coding is allowed, but not AI comments which I didn't. Some were even approved by maintainers.
Anyway thanks for the comments from the reviewers, at least I'll be able to refactor in my own repo and simplify my LaTeX document.

It seems I was the only maintainer interacting with your PRs, and I did not "approve" those I looked at. New contributors are not encouraged to use LLM to write PRs. Maintainers and reviewers have different opinions about AI, but some of us feel it is better to use our PR-reviewing time on humanly written PRs, especially for new contributors, who would learn how to improve their code and level up their future PRs. We do not have unlimited reviewing capacities. Your PRs really looked like a flood going in too many directions. "Mastering" one corner of mathlib is difficult enough!
See also https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/144837-PR-reviews/topic/.2345116.20rank.20via.20nonzero.20minors/near/633584054

Unfortunately you weren't the only to discuss @Joël Riou, just check the number of comments of the PR list I gave. I even suggested ways of how maintainers could manage the problem of volume.

#44721 was approved by wwylele for example
#44769 was also discussed very far and was more about to what point the reviewers wanted to generalize,

https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/#use-of-ai

  • If your PR contains a substantial amount of LLM-generated code, add the LLM-generated label by adding the comment LLM-generated.
  • Using an LLM when writing comments on GitHub or Zulip is not allowed: use your own words.

I think I did followed the two core rules, do you feel like discussing to a robot right now? What makes you think I didn't learn about Lean through the process? Can you also tell it didn't worked on the project I am working on since August and also the low quality of what was proposed in terms of maths?

In 2026, coding assistant is becoming as standard as having a keyboard, a screen or using autocompletion.
Source: AI usage section at https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2026
The fact that you are trying to contribute to many top folders of mathlib simultaneously does not inspire confidence in your claim that you are actually learning something about mathlib
If you truly want to learn how to contribute to mathlib, why not open one short PR containing material you understand well, and going through the review process without using any (further) LLM tools?
Somewhat relatedly, it would be good if you filled in your github handle in your Zulip profile, so that we can mentally match you across the two platforms
So you are saying I could just pick one PR, preferrably the most simple one, and ask someone to reopen it, that's sounds nice, not very different than having draft PR, but I can do that.
I think we're saying "do you want to learn how to write mathlib-quality code manually, and if you don't then you might be in the wrong place"

We are well aware that in 2026 having a coding assistant is the norm, but what you are unaware of is the current aims and objectives of mathlib, which are not "get all mathematics formalised as soon as possible". Do you know about Tau Ceti? https://taucetiproject.org/ This might be more aligned with what you are thinking.

But Yael just said I can open one short PR.
I indeed had the same kind of conversation in the formal-conjectures thread and started contributing TauCetiRoadmap repo as well for conjectures
Yael also said "If you truly want to learn how to contribute to mathlib".

For the set of closed PR, I will refactor the code to two Tauceti roadmaps.
Answer to your question is yes of course, you are assuming and presuming bad intentions but I really want to help.
Have you tried reading and working through #mil?

I wouldn't be here if I didn't read documentation and open the PRs obviously, "learn how to contribute to mathlib" :)

I can even have a 30min online interview with one of you if you want.
#mil is not even documentation...
What documentation are you referring to? The mathlib docs?
documentation, course
you used a python documentation framework to build MIL, that's how developers call the generated documentation

So I still don't get if you want me (you) to (re)open the few lines pull request, sorry please be clear about it to close the discussion.

You do realize this conversation is funny and feels like entering a dojo in karate kid and professor asking if I want to learn.
I studied maths until masters degree, and am an experimented developer, what do you need more to just open a pull request on a github repo.
You could have just answered "no I haven't read it yet"

I did!
You might want to update this if you feel these docs are important.
https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/how-to-contribute.html

If you have seen something shocking in my coding style @Weiyi Wang please let me know that makes you think I "don't want to learn" or I "didn't read documentation" I'll work on it.

All of this is again very subjective to contribute only 30 lines of code. What I am suspecting is that you need reference checks and diplomas etc. am I wrong?
Again, #mil is NOT documentation
This is not just about semantics. If you just assume it is, then your fundamental understanding of mathlib is wrong

"Theorem Proving in Lean* is for people who prefer to read a user manual cover to cover before using a new dishwasher"*

It even does the Dishwasher documentation comparison itself...
We've had plenty of undergraduates or people outside academia contribute to Mathlib; this is not inherently blocking.

Yaël Dillies said:

If you truly want to learn how to contribute to mathlib, why not open one short PR containing material you understand well, and going through the review process without using any (further) LLM tools?

What Yaël said here still applies. Feel free to do this.
if I proved you I read the MIL documentation book user manual in august would you believe me?

I already did this Yael, and people like Weiyi even commented it and validated the PR

Why not just reopen any of these three, instead of trying to prove I don't care.
#44730, #44756, #44721

Michel Hua said:

people like Weiyi even commented it and validated the PR

Deducing "somebody commented on it => the PR was found good" is not valid in general.

If I notice something on a pull request outside of my area of expertise, I may comment about that aspect --- which does not imply "the pull request is suitable for mathlib". If merely says "this aspect should be taken into account, and possibly be changed". (Even if, as a mathlib maintainer, I'm qualified to make this judgement in my areas of expertise.)

We are talking about high school maths. My github repo commits have track of me trying to learn lean since august, I think you don't have anything to say to that.

For the algebraic geometry stuff I am learning it, and it's from Grothendieck work, I even disprove part on the theorem in a modern textbook the other day thanks to Lean.
I'm no maintainer, but I think #44756 is by far the more polished out of those three (largely thanks to the reviews, mind you). If you want to follow Yaël's suggestion, that's the PR I'd recommend.

Last call, I spend the whole day debating with many people, it's in TauCetiRoadmap anyway, and will be proved by AI later.
https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pulls?q=is%3Apr+state%3Aopen+author%3Amycaule
